prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Walt Disney Co" (ticker DIS), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "DIS", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Walt Disney Company
markets: Linear TV networks (ABC, Disney Channel, FX, National Geographic)

mission.statement: The mission of The Walt Disney Company is to entertain, inform and inspire people around the globe through the power of unparalleled storytelling, reflecting the iconic brands, creative minds and innovative technologies that make ours the world's premier entertainment company.
mission.plain: Disney wants to delight and inspire people everywhere by telling great stories.

about.plain: Disney makes movies and TV shows, like Toy Story, Frozen, Marvel and Star Wars. People can watch them in cinemas, on TV channels like ABC and ESPN, or on its streaming apps Disney+ and Hulu. It also runs theme parks such as Disney World and Disneyland, hotels and cruise ships. And it earns money when other companies put its characters on toys, clothes and games.
about.customers: Families and fans around the world, plus advertisers, cable and TV companies, cinemas and toy makers that pay to use its shows and characters.
about.everyday: If you have watched a Pixar film, streamed Disney+, seen a game on ESPN or bought a Mickey Mouse T-shirt, you have used Disney.

money.plain: Park tickets, hotels, cruises, food, merchandise and licensing (Experiences revenue $36.2bn in FY2025)
Disney+ and Hulu subscriptions and ads ($24.6bn in FY2025)
ESPN channels, ESPN streaming and sports ads ($17.7bn in FY2025)
ABC, Disney Channel, FX and National Geographic channels paid for by cable companies and advertisers ($9.4bn in FY2025)
Cinema tickets, film and show sales to others ($8.5bn in FY2025)
The standalone ESPN app (launched August 2025), a $1.5bn stake in Epic Games and a $1bn investment and character licence with OpenAI's Sora (December 2025)

result.summary: Disney has one of the widest moats in entertainment, built on the world's most valuable library of characters and franchises (Disney, Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars) that it monetises again and again across films, streaming, theme parks and merchandise. Its parks are nearly impossible to copy and earned $10.0bn of operating income in FY2025, while streaming has turned profitable. The weak spots are the shrinking linear TV business, rising sports-rights costs and patchier box-office results.

pricingPower.evidence: Disney+ Premium was raised from $15.99 to $18.99 and the ad tier from $9.99 to $11.99 on October 21, 2025, yet streaming subscription revenue rose 15% and streaming operating income more than doubled to $712m in Q3 FY2026; in parks, average ticket revenue per guest rose 5% in Q3 FY2026 while worldwide attendance still grew 4%.

moats.evidence: Owns Disney, Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars, ESPN and National Geographic; Toy Story 5 passed $1bn at the global box office in 2026 and Disney was the No. 1 US distributor in 2025 with a 22.6% share (27.8% including 20th Century Studios).
Streaming subscribers can cancel any month and park visits are discretionary; only bundles (Disney+/Hulu/ESPN) and Disney Vacation Club timeshares add some stickiness.
The flywheel (films feed parks, merchandise and streaming) is a cross-selling advantage rather than a true network effect; more users do not make the product better for each other.

Spreads content costs over $94.4bn of revenue and about 196 million Disney+ and Hulu subscriptions (Sept 2025), and invests about $8bn a year in parks (FY2025 capex $8.0bn), a scale few rivals can match.
Destination theme-park markets like Orlando and Anaheim support only a few multi-billion-dollar resorts; Disney and Comcast's Universal are effectively the only global players.
Disney is the incumbent being disrupted by streaming and YouTube rather than a challenger with a model rivals cannot copy.

Walt Disney Imagineering and Pixar's storytelling process have decades of accumulated know-how in ride design, animation and guest operations, though recent live-action releases such as Moana and The Mandalorian and Grogu underperformed in 2026.
Exclusive ownership of character IP (Mickey, Marvel, Star Wars, Pixar) and long-term sports rights including the NFL, whose NFL Network deal closed in early 2026 giving the league 10% of ESPN.

customers.evidence: Parks keep drawing repeat visitors (worldwide attendance up 4% in Q3 FY2026 despite higher prices) and Disney+ grew subscription revenue 15% after an October 2025 price rise; complaints focus on high park prices and crowding.

talent.evidence: Disney remains a magnet for creative talent and ranked No. 13 on Fortune's 2025 World's Most Admired Companies list, but it slipped from No. 6 in 2023 and has had repeated layoffs and labour disputes at parks.

product.evidence: Disney parks are widely seen as the benchmark for the industry and Pixar/Disney Animation have won more animated-feature Oscars than any rival; Disney had the biggest share of US TV viewing among media companies at 11.9% in January 2026 (Nielsen, second only to YouTube).

competitors.name: Comcast (NBCUniversal, Universal Parks, Peacock)
competitors.note: Universal theme parks (Epic Universe opened in Orlando in 2025), Universal and DreamWorks films, NBC and Peacock streaming.

competitors.name: Netflix
competitors.note: Largest subscription streaming rival; competes for subscribers, talent and family content.

competitors.name: Skydance (Paramount + Warner Bros. Discovery)
competitors.note: Merged in 2026; owns Warner Bros., HBO Max, Paramount+, CBS, CNN, TNT Sports and DC, competing in film, streaming, sports and TV networks.

competitors.name: Alphabet (YouTube, YouTube TV)
competitors.note: YouTube is the biggest source of US TV viewing (12.5% in January 2026) and competes for viewing time and ad dollars; YouTube TV is a key ESPN distributor.

competitors.name: Amazon (Prime Video, MGM)
competitors.note: Prime Video streaming, MGM studio and sports rights such as NFL Thursday Night Football and the NBA.

competitors.name: Fox Corporation
competitors.note: Fox broadcast network and Fox Sports compete with ABC and ESPN for viewers, ads and sports rights; Tubi competes in free streaming.

competitors.name: Apple (Apple TV)
competitors.note: Apple TV streaming originals plus MLS and F1 rights.

competitors.name: Sony Group (Sony Pictures, PlayStation)
competitors.note: Film studio rival (it shares Spider-Man with Marvel) and video games competing for family entertainment time.

competitors.name: Six Flags Entertainment
competitors.note: Regional US theme parks competing for day visits and leisure spending.

competitors.name: Merlin Entertainments (Legoland, Madame Tussauds)
competitors.note: Private theme-park and attraction operator, including Legoland resorts in Florida, California and Europe.

competitors.name: Royal Caribbean Group
competitors.note: Competes with Disney Cruise Line for family cruise holidays.

competitors.name: Roku
competitors.note: Free ad-supported Roku Channel competes for viewing and connected-TV ad budgets; also a distribution partner.

competitors.name: ByteDance (TikTok)
competitors.note: Short-form video competes for young people's leisure time (Disney has also partnered with TikTok on Disney+ short videos in 2026).

competitors.name: Hasbro / Mattel (toys)
competitors.note: Own toy brands compete with Disney licensed merchandise, though both are also Disney licensees.

estimates.name: Paramount Skydance (before Warner Bros. Discovery merger)

marketShare.market: US/Canada box office by distributor (The Numbers; box-office years)

rows.name: Walt Disney Studios (Disney label; 20th Century Studios adds a further 5.2% in 2025)

marketShare.market: Share of total US TV viewing by media company (Nielsen Media Distributor Gauge, January 2026)

threats: Cord-cutting keeps shrinking the linear TV business: Linear Networks revenue fell from $10.7bn in FY2024 to $9.4bn in FY2025 and its operating income from $3.45bn to $2.96bn.
Rising sports-rights costs and the shift of ESPN to streaming: Sports operating income fell 17% in Q3 FY2026 even as ESPN viewership grew.
Stronger rivals: Skydance (Paramount plus Warner Bros. Discovery) combines HBO, Warner Bros. and DC, and Universal's Epic Universe opened in Orlando in 2025.
Creative misses: live-action Moana and The Mandalorian and Grogu underperformed in 2026, showing franchise fatigue risk.
Theme parks depend on consumer spending and travel; Disney cited weak international visitation to US parks in 2026, and heavy park capex (about $8bn in FY2025) must keep earning good returns.
YouTube, TikTok and AI-generated video compete for children's and young adults' attention.
Leadership transition: Josh D'Amaro replaced Bob Iger as CEO in March 2026 after years of succession turmoil.

ceo.name: Josh D'Amaro
ceo.background: Georgetown University business administration graduate; joined Disneyland Resort in 1998, ran Disneyland and Walt Disney World, and was Chairman of Disney Experiences from 2020 before becoming CEO on March 18, 2026.

c1.evidence: Disney leads mature industries (theme parks, family film) and is a top player in streaming, which is still growing (streaming revenue +11% in Q3 FY2026), but it is not the leader of a fast-emerging industry; Netflix and YouTube lead streaming viewing.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Disney for characters and stories they love (Disney, Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars) and for park experiences no one else can offer; that IP is owned outright and has lasted for a century, so it is very hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Disney is one of the most recognised names on earth and the default choice for family entertainment and theme-park holidays; it was the No. 1 US box-office distributor in 2025.

c4.evidence: Its mission to 'entertain, inform and inspire people around the globe through the power of unparalleled storytelling' is meaningful and repeated, but recent management has been focused heavily on cost cuts, streaming profitability and buybacks ($7bn target for FY2026).

c6.evidence: “magical, family-friendly, nostalgic, expensive” — the public impression is mostly positive and warm, tempered by complaints about rising park prices and political controversies of recent years.

c7.evidence: Global entertainment, streaming and travel are large and growing with rising middle classes, but linear TV is in secular decline and analysts expect Disney's revenue to grow only around 5-6% a year.

c8.evidence: Disney is expanding into a new Abu Dhabi theme park (announced 2025), more cruise ships, ESPN streaming, games (a $1.5bn Epic Games stake) and AI-powered fan content through its $1bn OpenAI deal.

m1.evidence: D'Amaro has set a clear aim for Disney+ to become 'the digital centerpiece of The Walt Disney Company' and led the parks' big expansion plan, but he has been CEO only since March 2026 and is seen as an operator more than a visionary.

m2.evidence: D'Amaro is not a founder but a 28-year Disney lifer who rose from Disneyland Resort and is known for passion about the guest experience; it is too early to judge a founder-like long-term track record as CEO.

m4.evidence: D'Amaro built his reputation as a visible, people-focused parks leader who spends time with cast members and guests, and his Experiences unit delivered record income above $10bn in FY2025.

m5.evidence: He oversaw Imagineering's pipeline of new attractions, but as a new CEO there is not yet evidence that he has reshaped company-wide culture toward invention.

m6.evidence: D'Amaro is very hands-on with parks and attractions, but his background is business administration, finance and operations, not engineering.

m7.evidence: No public controversies and a reputation for integrity, but there is not yet a record as CEO showing stewardship aimed at causes beyond the company.

m7b.evidence: No verified commencement speech by D'Amaro at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: He is known as a charismatic, upbeat presence at park events and fan conventions, but he is not a widely famous public personality like Musk or Karp.

m9.evidence: As head of Disney Experiences from 2020, he grew the unit to $36.2bn revenue and $10.0bn operating income in FY2025; his first full quarter as CEO (Q3 FY2026) delivered 7% revenue growth and adjusted EPS of $2.06 versus $1.61.

m10.evidence: Disney is not known for frugality; it spends heavily on content, parks (about $8bn capex in FY2025) and executive pay, though it has run large cost-cutting programmes since 2023.

c10.evidence: Disney brings joy to hundreds of millions of people worldwide through films, streaming and parks, but entertainment improves lives less fundamentally than search or medical devices.

p2.evidence: Building global franchises and parks like Disney World is extremely hard to replicate, but entertainment is important to culture rather than essential to the world.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from FY2020 to FY2025: $65.4bn, $67.4bn, $82.7bn, $88.9bn, $91.4bn and $94.4bn.

f2.evidence: Total segment operating margin rose from 12.4% in FY2020 ($8.1bn on $65.4bn) to 18.6% in FY2025 ($17.6bn on $94.4bn), driven by parks growth and streaming turning profitable, with a dip in FY2021.

f3.evidence: At June 27, 2026 borrowings were $46.0bn against $5.2bn cash, about 4.6 times FY2025 free cash flow of $10.1bn, though Disney shareholders' equity was a healthy $110.0bn.

f4.evidence: Cash from operations rose from $7.6bn in FY2020 to $18.1bn in FY2025 and total segment operating income from $8.1bn to $17.6bn.

v1.evidence: Disney parks are clearly the best in their field for families, but in streaming Netflix and YouTube attract more viewing, so its main businesses are not all the obvious best choice.

v2.evidence: Disney was No. 13 on Fortune's 2025 World's Most Admired Companies list and remains a dream employer for creatives, but it fell from No. 6 in 2023 and has had layoffs and pay disputes with park workers.

c5.evidence: Families worldwide would miss Disney's films, characters and parks, which are part of childhood memories for generations, though rivals could fill some entertainment needs.
